annotations.keyFindings: Structured codes made recommendations more specific (46 to 88 percent naming modality and interval), and completion rose from 51 to 58 percent; completion was lowest for emergency department examinations.
annotations.limitations: Before-after in one department; codes notified no one; imaging done elsewhere was missed.

annotations.keyFindings: With a nurse navigator, completion within the window was 79 percent against 43 percent the year before, and 64 percent among patients without a regular primary care clinician; one full-time navigator handled about 800 new nodules a year.
annotations.limitations: Compared with one earlier year; lung nodules only; no adjustment for referral changes.

annotations.keyFindings: Completion was 62 percent at the alert hospital and 55 percent at the comparison hospital; alerts were acknowledged within seven days for 71 percent of findings, but for 38 percent when the ordering clinician was an emergency physician or a rotated resident.
annotations.limitations: Two hospitals with different patient mix and primary care access.

annotations.keyFindings: Letters to patients were followed by completion of 60 percent against 48 percent in a matched earlier group; 17 percent of responding patients said the letter made them very worried.
annotations.limitations: Historical matched comparison; 212 of 390 questionnaires returned; English-only letters.

annotations.keyFindings: Across 37 reports, the loop most often broke where no clinician took responsibility, where recommendations were vague, where patients were seen only in emergency or inpatient settings, and after patients moved.
annotations.limitations: Quality of the included reports not assessed; mostly single academic centres; language barriers rarely described.

annotations.keyFindings: Completion within one year was 67 percent for patients with a primary care clinician and 34 percent for those without, most of whom were first imaged in the emergency department.
annotations.limitations: One health system's records; imaging done elsewhere not captured.

annotations.keyFindings: A combined programme of codes, a tracking list and navigators saw completion rise from 49 to 76 percent over five years, needing 2.5 full-time staff.
annotations.limitations: No comparison system; introduced in stages with other safety work, so components cannot be separated.

claims.text: With a nurse navigator for incidental lung nodules, follow-up completion within the recommended window was 79 percent, against 43 percent in the year before, and 64 percent among patients without a regular primary care clinician.
claims.passage: Follow-up completion within the recommended window was 79 percent, compared with 43 percent in the year before the navigator started.
claims.interpretation: A named person closing the loop is associated with the largest reported gain; the comparison is with a single earlier year.

claims.text: Automated alerts to ordering clinicians were associated with completion of 62 percent against 55 percent at a comparison hospital, and acknowledgement fell to 38 percent when the ordering clinician was an emergency physician or a rotated resident.
claims.passage: When the ordering clinician was an emergency physician or a resident who had since rotated, acknowledgement fell to 38 percent.
claims.interpretation: Alerts depend on a clinician who is still responsible for the patient.

claims.text: For incidental adrenal or renal lesions, follow-up completion within one year was 67 percent for patients with a primary care clinician and 34 percent for those without.
claims.passage: Follow-up completion within one year was 67 percent for patients with a primary care clinician and 34 percent for those without.
claims.interpretation: Patients without a primary care clinician need an approach that does not rely on one.

claims.text: A review of 37 reports found the loop most often broke where no clinician took responsibility, where recommendations were vague, where patients were seen only in emergency or inpatient settings, and after patients moved.
claims.passage: The most frequent failure points were a recommendation that did not reach a clinician who took responsibility, vague recommendations without a modality or interval, patients seen only in emergency or inpatient settings without a follow-up clinician, and loss of contact after patients moved.
claims.interpretation: The review can be organised by these failure points.

synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Approaches that assign a person to close the loop report the largest gains (a navigator: 79 against 43 percent), clinician alerts help less when the ordering clinician is no longer responsible (acknowledgement 38 percent for emergency physicians and rotated residents), and letters to patients raise completion while worrying some patients. Patients without a primary care clinician complete follow-up far less often (34 against 67 percent), and the loop breaks at predictable points. Completion is defined with different windows and denominators, so figures cannot be pooled. The four model leads, including a national benchmark presented as a landmark, were not retrieved and are not part of this appraisal.
gradeRationale: Before-after and two-site comparisons from single systems, a structured review without quality assessment, and descriptive records; consistent in direction but at serious risk of bias and not comparable across definitions.
summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; four source-derived claims; overall certainty low; the leads are not appraised.
